rv.q: The whole thing is pretty odd, and yet oddly fun. Or, as Elling likes to say whenever people catch on that he is a little odd, "I prefer the English expression 'rare.' As in uncommon."
Elling has just enough edge to keep itself from falling into a sugar coma; the story’s already mild politics have been muted to a murmur in this adaptation.
Like its characters, “Elling” doesn’t quite fit in its natural environment, but it has a modest, oddball charm.

But as dumbed down for American auds (why do they keep doing this to us?), this queasy-making comedy is so broadly played, by a cast headlined by Denis O’Hare and Brendan Fraser, it’s close to sitcom.
The Elling and Kjell Bjarne who prove such moving, gently amusing company in the movie are rendered overbearing and charmless onstage.
Everything is pitched so loud that nuances of character and emotional underpinnings get lost, which draws attention to the play's fragile dramatic trajectory.
"Elling" is relentlessly sentimental and comprehensively unfunny, so much so that I had to struggle to stay awake all the way to the bitter end.
Free Man evolves from a bustling farce into something deeper and darker but similarly exhilarating.
But like its marquee star, Elling doesn't feel quite ready for the Broadway stage.
"Gods and Monsters" alum Fraser lets his demented side show in his vanity-free turn.
It's just that it's so flabby, flimsy, and undercooked that even most four-star sushi restaurants would balk at it.
Better yet, take pity on the audience that needs to sit through this misconceived mishap.

The story of two recently released mental patients bunking together in an apartment in Oslo doesn’t sound like perfect fodder for a Broadway comedy. But there’s something relentlessly charming about "Elling."
Unfortunately, Bent drags their uneventful doings out for two acts and director Doug Hughes' wishy-washy production generates only intermittent laughs and scant emotional resonance.

cn.t: Critics are mixed on this Norwegian odd-couple comedy about two mental patients adjusting to life outside an institution. While some find it charming and endearing, others criticize it as coarsened for Broadway, with Fraser's debut drawing particular scrutiny.
